abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a foundational revision of effect typing in functional programming languages, challenging the conventional wisdom that effects must be tracked through monadic type annotations. We introduce the **Suspension Calculus (SC)**, a novel theoretical framework that treats effectful computations as first-class values without explicit monadic wrapping. The key insight is that effects can be safely encapsulated through a continuation-passing transformation combined with kind-indexed effect signatures, enabling polymorphic effect handlers that preserve parametricity. We develop the metatheory of SC, proving type safety, effect isolation, and strong normalization under suitable restrictions. The framework naturally subsumes existing effect systems while enabling previously impossible program transformations, such as effect polymorphism over higher-order functions. Our formal development reveals deep connections between delimited continuations, effect handlers, and linear logic that were obscured in prior formulations. We demonstrate that the suspension approach resolves long-standing paradoxes in effect intersection and subeffecting, providing a cleaner semantic foundation for practical effect handlers as found in languages like Koka and Eff. This work fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between pure functional programming and computational effects.

We present a novel type-theoretic characterization of resource-aware programming in the lambda calculus, significantly extending the capabilities of previous affine and linear type systems. Our **Graded Monadic Framework (GMF)** combines graded monads with quantitative type theory to track not just whether a resource is used, but precisely how and when it is accessed. Unlike prior work that addresses either space or time properties in isolation, GMF provides a unified treatment enabling compositional reasoning about both dimensions through a single type annotation scheme. We develop a syntactic soundness proof showing that well-typed programs cannot violate resource bounds, and a semantic characterization establishing connections to proven resource analysis tools. The framework supports higher-order functions, polymorphism, and recursive types while maintaining decidable type-checking. Our work improves upon existing graded type systems by eliminating their restriction to first-order programs and by providing a clean categorical semantics based on enriched Lawvere theories. We demonstrate practical applicability through case studies in embedded systems programming and differential privacy, showing that GMF enables precise resource certification at the type level.

This paper introduces **Fibjs**, a domain-specific functional programming language designed from first principles for high-performance concurrent systems. Fibjs reimagines cooperative concurrency for functional languages by combining first-class delimited continuations with a linear type system that ensures effect purity across suspension points. Unlike existing approaches that bolt concurrency onto pure functional foundations through monadic embeddings or green threads, Fibjs treats asynchronous computation as a primitive linguistic construct supported by a novel effect region system. The language includes a fully implemented compiler targeting native code, a comprehensive standard library with native interop, and a rich module system supporting hierarchical name spaces. We present empirical evaluations showing that Fibjs programs achieve throughput competitive with event-driven systems while maintaining the compositionality and equational reasoning properties expected of functional languages. The design space exploration reveals that functional concurrency primitives, when properly integrated with affine capabilities, can provide both safety guarantees and performance characteristics superior to conventional callback-based or async/await approaches. This work demonstrates a viable path toward practical purely functional programming in high-throughput server environments.

We present **GenCast**, a substantially improved generic programming library for Haskell that overcomes fundamental limitations in existing approaches to datatype-generic functions. GenCast is built on a novel composition mechanism for type-level representations that enables truly modular generic functions without requiring the elaborate type-level programming necessary in Scrap Your Boilerplate or Generic Deriving. The key innovation is the **Stratified Representation (SR)**, a two-level type structure that cleanly separates the structural description of datatypes from their interpretation, enabling independent development and composition of both. Our implementation includes a robust Template Haskell elaboration engine that handles the full GADT extension of Haskell, including existentially quantified types and type families. We provide an extensive library of generic operations covering serialization, parsing, pretty-printing, and structure editing, demonstrating that GenCast significantly reduces boilerplate compared to hand-written implementations while maintaining competitive performance. Benchmarks on real-world codebases show average reductions of 60% in development effort with only 15% runtime overhead compared to optimized handwritten equivalents. The library integrates seamlessly with existing Haskell tooling and has been deployed in production systems processing millions of daily transactions.
